title: Superficial Thrombophlebitis
subject: Medicine
summary: Superficial thrombophlebitis is inflammation of a superficial vein with a thrombus, often secondary to infection, trauma or hypercoagulability. In low‑resource settings common causes include skin infections, HIV‑related vasculitis and herbal irritants. Prompt recognition prevents extension to deep veins and sepsis.

sections.p: A tender, cord‑like, erythematous vein segment, usually in the lower limb, with a palpable induration. Diagnosis is clinical; duplex ultrasound confirms thrombus and excludes deep vein involvement.
b: Tender, warm cord following a superficial vein
Redness extending <5 cm from the cord
No signs of deep vein thrombosis (no calf swelling, normal Homan's sign)

sections.p: Three grades guide management: Grade 1 – limited to a short segment, no systemic signs; Grade 2 – >5 cm, mild fever or leukocytosis; Grade 3 – extensive, fever >38 °C, or signs of infection/extension.
b: Grade 1: outpatient, local care
Grade 2: consider short‑course antibiotics, monitor
Grade 3: admit, treat as septic thrombophlebitis

sections.p: In East African hospitals the most frequent precipitants are skin and soft‑tissue infections, intravenous cannulation, and HIV‑related vasculitis. Other causes follow.
b: Local bacterial infection (streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus)
IV catheter or peripheral line trauma
HIV‑associated vasculitis or opportunistic infection
Malaria‑related endothelial activation
Herbal or topical irritants
Hypercoagulable states (e.g., sickle cell, antiphospholipid syndrome)

sections.p: Patients report a painful, red line that may have appeared after a minor injury or IV insertion. Fever, chills, or malaise suggest progression to septic thrombophlebitis.
b: Localized pain worsening with movement
Erythema and induration along the vein
Low‑grade fever (often <38 °C) in early disease
Systemic signs (high fever, rigors) in Grade 3

t.b: Confirms superficial thrombus and excludes deep vein thrombosis; if unavailable, rely on clinical exam and treat conservatively.
Detects leukocytosis (>10 ×10⁹/L) indicating infection; normal count does not exclude early disease.
Indicated if fever >38 °C or systemic signs; isolates guide antibiotic choice.
Identifies HIV‑related vasculitis as a precipitant; results may be delayed—manage empirically if high suspicion.

sections.p: Extension into deep veins, septic emboli, cellulitis, and necrotising fasciitis are life‑threatening.
b: Rapid increase in swelling or pain
High fever (>38 °C) or rigors
Signs of systemic sepsis (hypotension, tachycardia)
New calf tenderness suggesting DVT

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide local care, and use anticoagulation only when deep veins are involved or there is high risk of propagation.
b: Warm compresses and elevation of the limb
Analgesia with NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) unless contraindicated
Empiric oral antibiotics covering Staph and Strep (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) for suspected infection
If septic signs, give IV ceftriaxone or cloxacillin; avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy
Consider low‑dose LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) only if ultrasound shows deep extension or patient has pro‑thrombotic risk
Avoid systemic anticoagulation in isolated superficial disease without risk factors

sections.p: Re‑examine after 5‑7 days; ensure resolution of cord and absence of new swelling. Prevent recurrence by avoiding unnecessary IV cannulation and treating skin infections promptly.
b: Repeat bedside exam; ultrasound only if symptoms persist
Educate patient on early signs of infection
Use aseptic technique for all venous access
Treat underlying HIV or sickle‑cell disease aggressively

sections.p: Deep vein thrombosis, cellulitis, and Buerger disease can mimic superficial thrombophlebitis.
b: DVT – calf swelling, positive Homan's sign, requires anticoagulation
Cellulitis – diffuse erythema without a palpable cord
Thromboangiitis obliterans – affects small/medium arteries, smokers, distal ischemia

sections.p: Normal leukocyte count does not rule out early infection; CRP may be modest in immunocompromised patients.
b: Early infection can have normal WBC
HIV patients may have blunted inflammatory markers

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of systemic sepsis (low BP, tachycardia)

faq.a: No. It is reserved for extensive disease, deep vein extension, or high thrombotic risk.

faq.q: Can a superficial thrombophlebitis become a pulmonary embolism?
faq.a: Rarely, only if the thrombus propagates into the deep venous system.

faq.q: What is the role of compression stockings?
faq.a: They help reduce venous stasis after the acute phase but are not a primary treatment.

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with a painful red cord on his thigh after a peripheral IV. What is your immediate management? — Assess for systemic signs, start local care and empiric antibiotics; obtain ultrasound if deep extension is suspected.
How would you differentiate superficial thrombophlebitis from cellulitis on examination? — Look for a palpable, tender cord following a vein; cellulitis lacks a discrete cord and has diffuse edema.

A patient with a 6‑cm inflamed superficial vein has a temperature of 38.2 °C and leukocytosis. Which investigations are essential? — Duplex ultrasound to rule out DVT, blood cultures, CRP, and HIV test if status unknown.
Why is full‑dose anticoagulation avoided in isolated superficial thrombophlebitis? — The risk of bleeding outweighs the low embolic risk when the thrombus is confined to superficial veins.
What complications should you monitor for during admission for septic thrombophlebitis? — Progression to deep vein thrombosis, septic emboli, necrotising fasciitis, and systemic sepsis.
In a low‑resource setting without ultrasound, how would you decide whether to admit a patient? — Use clinical severity (fever >38 °C, >5 cm cord, systemic signs) to guide admission.

What preventive measures reduce recurrence of superficial thrombophlebitis in this population? — Proper skin hygiene, aseptic IV insertion, early treatment of skin infections, and control of HIV or sickle‑cell disease.
